name: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. & GEICO Indemnity Co. v. Barnor-Cooper
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed the denial of summary judgment to State Farm and GEICO in a UM claim arising from a hit-and-run collision, holding the plaintiff was not entitled to UM benefits under either policy. Injured while making a delivery in a Turo-rented Buick, she was not an insured under the State Farm policy: the Buick was not a "temporary substitute car" because the scheduled vehicle it would have replaced had been sold, and the named-insured LLC is a separate legal entity from its members and managers.
why: Reads the 'temporary substitute car' and named-insured provisions strictly: a borrowed vehicle is not a temporary substitute once the scheduled car it would replace has been sold, and an LLC policyholder is a separate legal entity from its members and managers, which narrows who qualifies as an insured for UM purposes.

name: Johnson v. Everett
synopsis: In a medical-malpractice case that ended in a defense verdict, the Court of Appeals held that the trial court mistakenly believed it had no choice but to let the jury consider the emergency-medical-care gross-negligence standard of O.C.G.A. § 51-1-29.5, an issue the parties had not listed in their pretrial order, when in fact the court had discretion to disallow it. The court vacated the denial of a new trial and remanded for the court to exercise that discretion, and found no error in admitting the defense expert's opinions or a complaint from another case.
why: A pretrial order frames the issues for trial, but the court keeps discretion over an issue the parties left out of it, and treating that discretion as nonexistent is reversible error.

name: Loveless v. GSH Investments, LLC
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed summary judgment for an apartment owner whose tenant's visitor was injured when an exterior wooden staircase collapsed, and affirmed the denial of the plaintiff's motions to compel. Before buying the complex the owner received an appraisal and an insurer survey flagging below-average condition and deferred maintenance, yet it never inspected the building exteriors or the stairways and kept no formal inspection process, relying on tenants to report problems. That evidence created a jury question on whether the owner had constructive knowledge of the hazard.
why: Prior reports flagging below-average condition, combined with the owner's lack of any inspection routine, can supply constructive knowledge of a hazard and create a jury question that defeats summary judgment.

name: Cannon v. Safeco Insurance Co. of Illinois
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal of a failure-to-settle action against a liability insurer. After a $1.65 million excess judgment was entered against its insured following a fatal collision, the insured alleged that Safeco had interpleaded and tendered its $100,000 limits into the court registry without obtaining any release of the claims against him. Because an insurer must give equal consideration to the insured's interests and may be liable for an excess judgment for a negligent or bad-faith failure to settle, the complaint stated a claim.
why: Tendering policy limits by interpleader, without obtaining a release for the insured, does not by itself discharge the insurer or bar a later failure-to-settle or bad-faith claim.

name: Sullivan v. Trustgard Insurance Co.
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed partial summary judgment that had set uninsured-motorist limits at $100,000 on a commercial auto policy. The insurer's application directed that its uninsured-motorist selection section was not to be used in Georgia and required a state-specific supplement, and neither that section nor the mandatory offer form was signed or initialed. Because the insurer never obtained a valid written election of reduced limits, the court held the coverage defaulted to the $1 million liability limit.
why: Without a compliant, signed election of reduced uninsured-motorist limits, the coverage defaults to the bodily-injury liability limit under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11.

name: Radheshvar, LLC v. Perez Larios
synopsis: The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of summary judgment to a motel owner in a premises case brought by a guest's social visitor who was attacked in a breezeway. The owner argued the visitor was a licensee owed only a duty to avoid wilful or wanton injury, but the court held a jury could find he was an invitee, leaving the applicable standard of care for the factfinder.
why: Invitee-versus-licensee status under O.C.G.A. §§ 51-3-1 and 51-3-2 is often a jury question, which can leave the standard of care for the factfinder and preclude summary judgment.

name: Giles v. Greenhouse Apartments, LLC
synopsis: The Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for an apartment owner and its manager in a negligent-security action by a tenant beaten by unknown assailants on the property in 2020. The landlord conceded it owed the tenant a duty of ordinary care; the affirmance rests solely on causation — the tenant could not establish that any claimed security failure proximately caused the attack — and, given that holding, the court expressly declined to reach the equal-or-superior-knowledge and assumption-of-risk defenses and the challenge to excluded evidence of other crime in the area.
why: Causation is an independently dispositive element of a negligent-security claim: a defendant can win summary judgment without litigating foreseeability at all. The incident predates SB 68, so the common-law framework applies; for incidents on or after April 21, 2025 the analysis runs through the statutory regime at O.C.G.A. §§ 51-3-50 to 51-3-57.
editor_note: Summary corrected 2026-06-11 after re-validation against the opinion: the holding rests on causation alone; the equal-or-superior-knowledge and assumption-of-risk defenses were expressly not reached.

name: Mejia v. SK Battery America, Inc.
synopsis: In a wrongful-death action arising from a fatal fall at a battery-plant construction site, the Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for the premises defendants on assumption of the risk, analyzed as an affirmative defense. The decedent, a foreman, had actual knowledge of the specific hazard — twelve days earlier he had watched a coworker fall through the same red-taped, non-weight-bearing louvers — and he stepped onto them without tying off and fell over fifty feet; his repeated safety training and written hazard acknowledgment supplied secondary support for the defense.
why: Actual knowledge drawn from witnessing a prior, identical accident can establish assumption of the risk as a matter of law; documentation like training records and signed acknowledgments corroborates the defense rather than carries it.
editor_note: Summary corrected 2026-06-11 after a re-validation flag: assumption of risk is the dispositive affirmative defense, grounded primarily in the decedent's eyewitness knowledge of a prior identical fall.

name: Venetian Hills Apartments, LLC v. Hughes
synopsis: In a wrongful-death action after a tenant died in a fire set during an assault by another tenant's guest, the Court of Appeals held the landlord was not entitled to judgment notwithstanding the verdict: it could be liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after parting with possession, and the criminal acts did not demand a defense verdict. The court nonetheless vacated the judgment and ordered a full retrial because the jury charges conflated landlord-tenant and premises-liability law.
why: A landlord can remain liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after giving up possession, but jury charges that blend § 44-7-14 with § 51-3-1 premises law can require a full retrial.

name: Williams v. Reddick
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed summary judgment for a defendant driver in a tractor-trailer collision case. The plaintiff had signed a limited liability release under O.C.G.A. § 33-24-41.1 that preserved claims to the extent other insurance was available, and a fact question remained on whether the employer's policy provided uninsured-motorist coverage, because an undated coverage summary did not establish a valid written rejection under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3).
why: A limited liability release under O.C.G.A. § 33-24-41.1 does not end the case where other coverage may exist, and a written uninsured-motorist rejection under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3) must actually appear in the record to be effective.

name: SMG Construction Services, LLC v. Cook
synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia vacated a Court of Appeals decision that had reversed summary judgment for a property owner whose independent contractor fell from an exposed second-story ledge. The Court held the Court of Appeals conflated actual and constructive knowledge and wrongly used constructive-knowledge principles to create a fact question about the contractor's actual knowledge of the open, unguarded ledge. Because the lower court stopped there, it had not addressed all elements of the owner's defenses, so the case was remanded.
why: Actual knowledge of an open and obvious hazard is analyzed on its own terms under O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1 and is not blurred into the constructive-knowledge inquiry; this is the decision the Mejia panel applied.

name: Ferriero v. Progressive Premier Insurance Co.
synopsis: The Court of Appeals vacated the dismissal of a collision suit for failure to serve the defendant. The plaintiff had served Progressive as her uninsured-motorist carrier and pointed to a process server's affidavit and email showing copies left with the defendant's mother, and the trial court abused its discretion in finding no evidence of substitute service under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-4(e)(7) when that evidence was in the record.
why: Substitute-service proof under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-4(e)(7) that is in the record must be addressed before dismissing for lack of service, and once the limitation period has run the case turns on the plaintiff's diligence in perfecting service.

name: John Doe v. Jones
synopsis: The Court of Appeals reversed the denial of partial summary judgment to a John Doe defendant, litigated in the name of the homeowners' uninsured-motorist carrier, after a phantom vehicle allegedly forced another driver into the plaintiffs' house. The plaintiff sought emotional-distress damages without a physical injury, and under Mayorga v. Benton he could not recover on a pecuniary-loss theory based on property damage alone.
why: Under Mayorga v. Benton, a plaintiff cannot recover emotional-distress damages without a physical injury on a pecuniary-loss theory based on property damage alone, here in a John Doe uninsured-motorist posture.

name: Walmart Stores East, LP v. Leverette
synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia vacated a $1 million "nominal damages" award in a premises injury case in which a shopper was struck by a heavy box. The Court held that nominal damages under Georgia law remain only a trivial sum, as at common law, and overruled the Court of Appeals precedent treating nominal damages as having no maximum. Because a million dollars is not a trivial sum, the judgment was vacated, with the remedy and invited-error questions left for the courts below.
why: Nominal damages under Georgia law remain only a trivial sum, and the Court overruled precedent that had treated them as having no ceiling, so a seven-figure 'nominal' award cannot stand.

name: Patterson v. United Services Automobile Association
synopsis: The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of uninsured-motorist coverage to an insured who was struck as a pedestrian and sought UM benefits from USAA. The policy required prompt notice as a condition precedent, and a twenty-one-month delay in notifying the insurer failed that requirement as a matter of law, with the insured's unawareness that UM coverage might apply not excusing the delay.
why: A prompt-notice condition precedent in a first-party uninsured-motorist policy can be enforced as a matter of law, and a long, unexplained reporting delay, here twenty-one months, can forfeit coverage even if the insured did not realize UM might apply.

name: Phillips v. Harmon
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded
synopsis: In a medical malpractice action, the Supreme Court of Georgia clarified that a defendant's duty to preserve evidence is triggered not only by actual or express notice of a claim from the plaintiff but whenever litigation is reasonably foreseeable to the party in control of the evidence, and that constructive notice may be shown by circumstances including the type and extent of injury, the clarity of fault, potential financial exposure, the frequency of litigation in similar circumstances, and the defendant's own conduct such as internal investigations and notification of counsel and insurers. The Court reversed the spoliation portion of the Court of Appeals judgment because the lower courts rested on the legally incorrect premise that actual notice from the plaintiff was required, and disapproved several Court of Appeals decisions to the extent they endorsed that analysis. The Court separately affirmed that the trial judge's ex parte communication with the deadlocked jury, conducted outside the presence of the parties and counsel and never disclosed before the verdict, violated the civil parties' right to be present and, under the unique circumstances including the inability to reconstruct the note, constituted harmful error requiring a new trial.
why: The decision reframes the trigger for a defendant's evidence-preservation duty around a reasonable-foreseeability standard with enumerated factors, disapproving prior precedent that required actual notice, and confirms that substantive ex parte judge-jury communications in civil trials can require a new trial.

name: Toyo Tire North America Manufacturing, Inc. v. Davis
synopsis: In a continuing nuisance and trespass action by homeowners against a nearby manufacturing facility, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that a plaintiff who both occupies and owns the affected property may recover separately for past discomfort and annoyance and for the diminution in the property's market value, treating these as two distinct injuries rather than a double recovery, and it expressly overruled Stanfield v. Waste Management of Georgia. The Court also held that alleged deficiencies in an expert appraiser's methodology go to the admissibility of his testimony under OCGA sections 24-7-702 and 24-7-703, an issue committed to the trial court's gatekeeping discretion in the first instance, and not to whether his opinion suffices to defeat summary judgment on causation. Because the defendant had not moved to exclude the expert testimony in the trial court, the appellate courts could consider that testimony in assessing whether causation survived summary judgment. The Court affirmed the denial of summary judgment.
why: The decision clarifies that past discomfort and annoyance damages and diminution in property value are separately recoverable in continuing nuisance cases and establishes that unchallenged expert testimony with methodological weaknesses may still be considered on summary judgment unless a Daubert exclusion motion is made to the trial court.

name: Scapa Dryer Fabrics, Inc. v. Knight
synopsis: In an asbestos mesothelioma case, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that an expert's cumulative exposure opinion, which told the jury that any exposure above background, even de minimis, was a contributing cause of the disease, did not 'fit' the legal causation standard and was inadmissible under former OCGA section 24-9-67.1 (b). The Court reaffirmed that, while a plaintiff need not prove a substantial contribution, a de minimis contribution does not satisfy Georgia's 'contributing factor' causation standard, and an expert must tie a cumulative exposure opinion to a reliable estimate of actual exposure showing more than de minimis exposure. Because the expert did not condition his causation opinion on such an estimate, its admission was an abuse of the trial court's gatekeeping discretion. The Court reversed the Court of Appeals' affirmance of the judgment.
why: The decision clarifies that expert causation testimony in toxic tort cases must satisfy the 'fit' requirement by being tied to a reliable estimate of more than de minimis exposure, and that an 'any exposure' or pure cumulative exposure theory unconnected to actual exposure is inadmissible.

name: Martin v. Six Flags Over Georgia II, L.P.
disposition: affirmed in part and reversed in part, and case remanded with direction
synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a premises owner can be liable under OCGA section 51-3-1 for a criminal attack that begins on its premises but is completed off-premises, when the injuries are a foreseeable proximate result of the owner's breach of its duty to keep the premises safe, expressly adopting the principle from Wilks v. Piggly Wiggly Southern. The court clarified that the bus stop where the attack concluded was not part of the park's 'approaches,' because the owner had not exercised the control and dominion required to extend its duty to that public way. On apportionment, the court held that an apportionment error under OCGA section 51-12-33 ordinarily requires a retrial limited to the apportionment of fault among tortfeasors, not a full retrial, because the allocation of relative fault is a step distinct from the determinations of liability and total damages. The court affirmed liability, reversed the Court of Appeals' order of a full retrial, and remanded for retrial limited to apportionment.
why: The decision establishes that off-premises injuries can support landowner liability where the attack originates on the premises and is foreseeable, clarifies the 'approaches' and control-and-dominion analysis, and holds that apportionment error generally requires retrial only on apportionment rather than a full retrial.

name: Cooper Tire & Rubber Company v. Koch
synopsis: In a product liability action arising from a fatal single-vehicle crash following a tire tread separation, the defendant tire manufacturer sought dismissal or other sanctions for spoliation after the plaintiff allowed the vehicle and remaining tires to be crushed for scrap. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the common-law duty to preserve relevant evidence is defined the same for plaintiffs and defendants, arising when a party actually anticipates or reasonably should anticipate litigation, though the practical timing of the duty may differ because plaintiffs generally control whether and when litigation is pursued. The court confirmed that the Phillips factors are a non-exclusive list, that the most severe sanctions are reserved for evidence lost intentionally in bad faith with uncurable prejudice, and that loss through mere negligence normally warrants lesser sanctions or none. Applying a summary judgment standard, the court affirmed the finding that the plaintiff had no duty to preserve at the time the evidence was destroyed.
why: The decision clarifies that the duty to preserve evidence and the reasonable-foreseeability test apply equally to plaintiffs and defendants, sets out how the Phillips factors and sophistication of the party bear on when that duty is triggered, and confirms that severe spoliation sanctions require intentional bad faith while negligent loss warrants lesser or no sanctions.

name: Quynn v. Hulsey
synopsis: In a wrongful death action arising from a truck striking and killing a pedestrian, the trial court granted partial summary judgment to the employer on the estate's claims for negligent entrustment, hiring, training, and supervision because the employer had admitted respondeat superior liability and no punitive damages claim survived. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the apportionment statute, OCGA section 51-12-33, abrogated the decisional law 'Respondeat Superior Rule,' which had entitled an employer that conceded vicarious liability to summary judgment on direct-negligence claims absent a valid punitive damages claim. The Court reasoned that direct-negligence claims allege the employer's own fault, which the jury must consider under the statute, and that such fault is divisible from the employee's fault. The Court reversed and overruled contrary Court of Appeals decisions.
why: The decision establishes that an employer's admission of respondeat superior no longer bars a plaintiff's negligent entrustment, hiring, training, supervision, and retention claims, so those direct-negligence claims may proceed to the jury alongside vicarious liability under OCGA section 51-12-33.

name: Adventure Motorsports Reinsurance, Ltd. v. Interstate National Dealer Services, Inc.
disposition: reversed and remanded in part, vacated and remanded in part
synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that vacatur of an arbitration award for manifest disregard of the law under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b) (5) requires concrete evidence that the arbitrator was conscious of the correct law and intentionally and knowingly chose to ignore it, and that a mere erroneous interpretation or misapplication of law to the facts does not suffice. Applying this standard, the court concluded that the arbitrator interpreted the parties' contracts and fashioned an equitable remedy that drew its essence from the agreements, and that nothing in the record showed a deliberate decision to disregard applicable law. The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision vacating the confirmation of the award and remanded for consideration of the unresolved argument under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b) (3) that the arbitrator overstepped his authority, and it vacated and remanded the related appeal concerning a delayed-payment penalty as potentially no longer moot.
why: The decision clarifies the demanding evidentiary threshold for vacating arbitration awards on manifest-disregard grounds under Georgia's Arbitration Code, an issue that recurs in disputes governed by arbitration clauses.

name: Miller v. Golden Peanut Company, LLC
synopsis: In a wrongful death action arising from a collision between a tractor-trailer and a car, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that the pre-2013 investigating officer rule, under which a law enforcement officer was treated as presumptively qualified as an expert on the cause of a collision, did not survive adoption of the current Evidence Code. Because OCGA section 24-7-702 contains no carve-out for law enforcement officers, a trial court must perform the same three-prong Daubert gatekeeping inquiry, qualification, reliability, and helpfulness, for expert opinion testimony from an investigating officer as for any other expert. The court found that the disputed accident-reconstruction opinions, including that the deceased driver was distracted, constituted expert rather than lay testimony, and that the trial court abused its discretion by assessing only qualification and not reliability or helpfulness. The court vacated the Court of Appeals' opinion, directed it to vacate the trial court's order, and remanded, and expressly disapproved Court of Appeals decisions applying the investigating officer rule to expert testimony in civil cases.
why: The decision establishes that investigating officers who offer accident-reconstruction or causation opinions in civil cases are subject to the full Daubert reliability and helpfulness analysis, eliminating the prior presumption of expert qualification.

name: Richardson v. Locklyn
synopsis: In an auto-collision case where the jury verdict came in below 75 percent of the defendant's rejected settlement offer, the trial court denied the defendant's motion for attorney fees under OCGA section 9-11-68 by finding the offer was not made in good faith based on the offer's relationship to claimed medical expenses and the defendant's stipulation to liability. The Court of Appeals held for the first time that an evidentiary hearing is required before a trial court may rule on a fee request under OCGA section 9-11-68, that a timely objection asserting bad faith triggers the hearing requirement, and that the burden rests on the offeree to prove the absence of good faith. Adopting Florida's framework, the court held that good faith cannot be assessed on objective factors alone but must consider the offeror's subjective reasonable belief, and it vacated the judgment and remanded for a hearing.
why: This decision establishes that an offeror's good faith under Georgia's offer-of-settlement statute is measured by the offeror's subjective reasonable belief rather than objective factors alone, places the burden on the offeree to show absence of good faith, and requires an evidentiary hearing triggered by a timely bad-faith objection.

name: Harris v. Mahone
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded with direction
synopsis: In an auto negligence case, plaintiff sought attorney fees under OCGA Section 9-11-68 after recovering a verdict exceeding 125 percent of his pretrial counteroffer. The court held that a counteroffer made within 20 days of trial under subsection (a) must still remain open 30 days under subsection (c), and that fees under subsection (b)(2) run only from the date the offer is deemed rejected through entry of judgment. Because the counteroffer was deemed rejected three days after the trial concluded and plaintiff showed no fees incurred in the window between that date and judgment, no fees were recoverable; a counteroffer can avoid this result only by being withdrawn in writing before its expiration. The court separately reversed the denial of fees under OCGA Section 9-15-14, holding that counsel's statement in his place as to hours and reasonableness on a specific issue was sufficient proof.
why: The decision clarifies the interplay of OCGA Section 9-11-68 subsections (a), (b)(2), and (c), holding that a near-trial counteroffer must remain open 30 days and that recoverable fees run only from the deemed-rejection date to judgment, and confirms that counsel's in-place statement of hours and reasonableness suffices to support a Section 9-15-14 fee motion.

name: Hospital Authority of Valdosta/Lowndes County v. Fender
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded
synopsis: In a medical malpractice action, the Court of Appeals held that a fact question existed on whether the new injury exception to the two-year statute of limitation in OCGA section 9-3-71(a) applied, where the patient remained asymptomatic for a period after an alleged misdiagnosis of carotid stenosis and later suffered a massive stroke, so the limitation period could begin on the date of the stroke. The court also held that the Respondeat Superior Rule, which entitles an employer to summary judgment on negligent hiring, training, supervision, and retention claims when it admits vicarious liability and no punitive damages are sought, was not superseded by the apportionment statute, OCGA section 51-12-33(b), reasoning that the statute does not apply to claims based on respondeat superior or to derivative claims that are merely duplicative of it. The court further affirmed denial of a motion under OCGA section 24-7-702(b) to exclude a medical expert's causation opinion. The court reversed summary judgment as to the negligent hiring claims and otherwise affirmed.
why: The decision clarifies that Georgia's apportionment statute does not displace the Respondeat Superior Rule barring direct negligence claims against an employer that admits vicarious liability and faces no punitive damages claim, and it applies the new injury exception to the medical malpractice limitation period where a misdiagnosed patient remains asymptomatic before a later distinct injury.

name: The Coastal Bank v. Rawlins
synopsis: After prevailing on appeal and obtaining a judgment of no liability, defendant moved for attorney fees under Georgia's offer of settlement statute, OCGA Section 9-11-68, based on a rejected $3,000 offer. The trial court denied fees, finding the offer was not made in good faith, but relied exclusively on objective factors such as the offer's relationship to alleged damages. The Court of Appeals held that under the test adopted in Richardson v. Locklyn, a court cannot base a good-faith ruling solely on objective factors but must weigh those factors against the offeror's subjective belief in the strength of its defense, here the no-standing argument. The court vacated and remanded for application of the Richardson test.
why: The decision clarifies that a good-faith determination under OCGA Section 9-11-68 requires weighing objective factors against the offeror's subjectively reasonable belief, and that exclusive reliance on objective factors is an abuse of discretion.

name: Stephens v. Castano-Castano
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part
synopsis: In an auto collision case, the trial court excluded evidence that the plaintiff's treating physician held a lien on the lawsuit proceeds and barred questioning about an attorney-to-physician referral. The Court of Appeals held that evidence of the physician's lien-based financial interest in the verdict was admissible to show potential bias and affect credibility, and that the collateral source rule did not bar it because the plaintiff still owed the full cost of treatment and no benefit or write-off reduced the obligation. The court affirmed exclusion of the attorney-referral evidence, holding that the referral standing alone was insufficient to show bias and presented a danger of unfair prejudice, and it affirmed denial of the defendant's motion to enforce a purported settlement because the relied-upon email omitted the essential settlement amount. The court noted that any such financial-interest evidence remains subject to a Rule 403 analysis. The opinion is physical precedent only.
why: The decision clarifies that a treating physician's lien on lawsuit proceeds is admissible to show financial interest and bias and is not barred by the collateral source rule, while a bare attorney-to-physician referral, standing alone, is not.

name: Aspen American Insurance Company v. Landstar Ranger, Inc.
synopsis: After a thief posing as a registered carrier stole a shipment, the cargo owner's insurer sued the transportation broker for negligent selection of the carrier, and the district court dismissed the claims as preempted by the FAAAA. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the FAAAA's express preemption provision bars state-law negligence claims against a broker based on carrier selection because such claims relate to a broker's service with respect to the transportation of property. The court further held that the FAAAA's safety exception does not save the claims because a broker's carrier-selection services have only an indirect, not a direct, connection to motor vehicles, so the claims are not 'with respect to motor vehicles.'
why: This decision establishes binding Eleventh Circuit authority that the FAAAA preempts state-law negligent-carrier-selection claims against freight brokers and that the safety exception does not apply to such broker claims, defining the scope of broker liability in trucking cases in the circuit.

treated_by.name: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC
treated_by.note: The later Supreme Court opinion holds that the FAAAA's safety exception does apply to state-law negligent-hiring claims against brokers because such claims are 'with respect to motor vehicles,' directly rejecting the Eleventh Circuit's contrary holding in the cited case that the safety exception does not save such claims.

treated_by.name: Willy Hodge v. Molson Coors Beverage Company USA, LLC
treated_by.note: The later opinion states that the cited decision's holding on FAAAA preemption of negligent-carrier-selection claims against brokers has been abrogated by an intervening Supreme Court decision and vacates a judgment that relied on it.

treatment_auto_note: Possibly abrogated by a later in-scope decision (Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC; Willy Hodge v. Molson Coors Beverage Company USA, LLC). Confirm on Shepard's.
editor_note: June 11, 2026: The Supreme Court answered. Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II abrogated this decision's FAAAA-preemption holding, and the Eleventh Circuit is already vacating judgments that relied on it (see the Hodge remand). Treatment upgrade to follow on Shepard's confirmation.
treatment_note: Overruled in part by Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC, 146 S. Ct. 1199 (2026); Shepard's confirmed June 12, 2026. The safety-exception holding is gone — negligent-hiring claims against brokers survive under 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c)(2)(A). Montgomery assumed without deciding the § 14501(c)(1) preemption-scope point Aspen also decided, and Aspen arose from cargo theft rather than personal injury.

name: GoAuto Insurance Company v. 2B Claims Services Inc.
synopsis: An insurer sued the third-party claims adjuster it hired, alleging the adjuster negligently failed to advise it about the risk of excess bad-faith liability after the insurer let a checks-in-hand policy-limits deadline pass and later settled for about $220,000 above the policy limits. Applying Florida bad-faith law, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the adjuster, holding that a claims adjuster has no duty to advise an insurer about its own legal risk of excess bad-faith exposure because such advice constitutes legal advice, and that the insurer's own decision to demand signed releases and not deliver the checks by the deadline, not the adjuster's conduct, proximately caused the excess settlement. The court noted the insurer knew of the checks-in-hand requirement eleven days before the deadline and could have delivered the checks.
why: The decision clarifies that a third-party claims adjuster owes no duty to advise an insurer about its own extracontractual bad-faith exposure and that an insurer's independent settlement and payment decisions, not the adjuster's handling, control causation in a negligence claim against the adjuster.

name: Vu v. City of Atlanta
synopsis: A city employee driving a city-owned truck rear-ended plaintiff's car, and plaintiff served a municipal ante litem notice demanding $1,000,000. The trial court dismissed the suit, accepting the city's argument that the notice failed to state a 'specific amount' under OCGA § 36-33-5(e) because it exceeded the $500,000 sovereign-immunity waiver for negligent motor-vehicle use. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that OCGA § 36-92-2 does not cap or limit the waiver but automatically waives immunity up to $500,000 while specifying ways to increase it, and reaffirming that the demanded amount need not be one the municipality is capable of accepting.
why: The decision clarifies that a municipal ante litem notice satisfies the specific-amount requirement of OCGA § 36-33-5(e) even when the demand exceeds the automatic sovereign-immunity waiver under OCGA § 36-92-2.

name: Ya Mon Expeditions, LLC v. YATCO, LLC
synopsis: In an interlocutory appeal from the denial of a motion to compel arbitration under the FAA, an MLS company sought to compel nonsignatory yacht-seller plaintiffs to arbitrate antitrust claims based on a subscription agreement their brokers allegedly accepted. The court held that under Florida law, which governs the threshold question of whether an arbitration agreement exists, the party seeking to compel arbitration bears the burden of proving an enforceable agreement, and the movant relied on speculation and assumption rather than evidence that the brokers actually listed the plaintiffs' yachts on its website or accepted the relevant version of the agreement. The court rejected the movant's argument that the nonsignatory plaintiffs opposing arbitration bore the burden of disproving its evidence.
why: It clarifies that the FAA presumption favoring arbitration does not apply to the threshold question of whether an agreement to arbitrate exists, and that state law places the burden of proving an enforceable arbitration agreement on the party seeking to compel it.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that the nonsignatory plaintiffs could not be bound to arbitrate under an agency-ratification theory. Applying the Florida Supreme Court's full-knowledge requirement, the court held that a principal ratifies an agent's pre-agency acceptance of a contract only on a showing that the principal had full knowledge of the agreement and its terms, and constructive knowledge does not suffice. Because the movant submitted no evidence that the plaintiffs knew of the agreement or its terms, and the brokers' knowledge could not be imputed because it was acquired before any agency relationship formed, ratification did not apply.
additional_holdings.why: It establishes that under controlling Florida Supreme Court precedent a nonsignatory principal cannot ratify an agent's pre-agency acceptance of an arbitration agreement absent full actual knowledge of the agreement and its terms.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that equitable estoppel did not bind the nonsignatory plaintiffs to arbitrate. A signatory may enforce an arbitration clause against a nonsignatory under equitable estoppel only if the nonsignatory relies on the agreement to assert its claims and the dispute falls within the clause. Because the plaintiffs' federal antitrust claims arose from statutory duties unrelated to the subscription agreement and did not require reference to or construction of that agreement, the plaintiffs were not claiming the benefits of the contract while avoiding its burdens.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that equitable estoppel cannot compel a nonsignatory to arbitrate where the asserted claims rest on independent statutory duties and do not depend on the contract containing the arbitration clause.

name: Allied Property & Casualty Insurance Company v. Bloodworth Wholesale Drugs Inc.
synopsis: Two pharmacies sued for their alleged role in the opioid epidemic sought defense and indemnity under liability and druggist liability policies covering damages 'because of bodily injury.' The insurers contended that the underlying government and healthcare suits seek economic losses not tied to identifiable injured persons and are therefore not covered, and the district courts granted summary judgment for the insurers. The Eleventh Circuit found no clear controlling Georgia or Florida precedent on whether such opioid lawsuits seek damages 'because of bodily injury,' distinguishing Georgia decisions like Cesnik, Lunceford, Presidential Hotel, and O'Dell as not dispositive. It certified to the Supreme Court of Georgia and the Supreme Court of Florida the question whether the policies require the insurers to defend and indemnify the insureds in the underlying opioid litigation.
why: The certification flags an unresolved, high-value coverage question of whether CGL and druggist liability policies covering 'damages because of bodily injury' reach opioid-epidemic suits seeking economic losses, leaving Georgia coverage law on the point to be settled by the Supreme Court of Georgia.

name: Waddle Trucking of Mississippi, Inc. v. Johnson
synopsis: A trucking defendant in a personal injury action was served in state court, after which a codefendant removed the case to federal court, where the defendant filed an answer that was untimely under Fed.R.Civ.P. 81(c)(2). After remand, the state court entered default judgment against the defendant. The Court of Appeals held that the answer filed in district court, even though untimely there, prevented default in state court because the district court never struck the answer and no default was entered under Fed.R.Civ.P. 55, and because on remand the defendant still had time remaining to answer.
why: The decision clarifies that an answer filed in federal court after removal continues to have effect on remand and prevents entry of default in state court so long as the federal court did not strike it or enter default, even if the federal answer was untimely.

name: Keathley v. Buddy Ayers Construction, Inc.
synopsis: A debtor in an open Chapter 13 bankruptcy failed to disclose a personal-injury claim arising from a car accident, and the lower courts applied judicial estoppel to bar the tort suit using the Fifth Circuit's two-factor test, asking only whether the debtor knew the underlying facts and had a potential motive to conceal. The Supreme Court, assuming without deciding that judicial estoppel can apply in the bankruptcy context and that inadvertence or mistake can be an exception, held that courts must look to the totality of the circumstances surrounding the omission. The Court found the Fifth Circuit's approach both too rigid, because equity eschews mechanical rules, and too broad, because its motive criterion is almost always satisfied, making it a poor fit for assessing whether an omission was actually inadvertent or mistaken.
why: It establishes that whether a plaintiff-debtor's failure to schedule a personal-injury claim was inadvertent or mistaken for judicial-estoppel purposes turns on the totality of the circumstances rather than a knowledge-plus-motive test, governing how civil litigants raise and defend against judicial estoppel when a tort claim was omitted from bankruptcy schedules.

name: Hodge v. Molson Coors Beverage Company USA, LLC
disposition: vacated in part, affirmed in part, and remanded
synopsis: A family injured by a semitruck sued a freight broker and a shipper, alleging negligent hiring of the carrier. The district court held that the FAAAA preempted the negligent-selection claim against the broker. Following the Supreme Court's decision in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, which abrogated the Eleventh Circuit's prior holding in Aspen American Insurance Co. v. Landstar Ranger, the court vacated and remanded, noting the district court had relied on now-abrogated caselaw.
why: It applies the Supreme Court's recent holding that the FAAAA does not preempt negligent-selection-of-carrier claims against brokers, abrogating prior Eleventh Circuit precedent that had foreclosed such claims.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court affirmed dismissal of the negligent-hiring claim against the shipper, applying Maryland law, which requires that the defendant's failure to undertake reasonable inquiry resulted in the contractor's hiring and that the hiring proximately caused the plaintiff's injury. The shipper hired Schneider, who hired Coyote, who hired the carrier, leaving the shipper three steps removed from hiring the operator. Because plaintiffs neither identified authority extending the theory that far nor alleged that the selection of Schneider was negligent, the claim failed, and influence over the hiring process was held not equivalent to actually hiring the carrier.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that negligent-hiring liability under Maryland law does not extend to a party several contractual layers removed from the entity that hired the operator absent an allegation tying the harm to the directly hired contractor.

name: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC
synopsis: An injured motorist sued a transportation broker for negligent hiring, alleging that the broker selected a motor carrier with a subpar federal safety rating that was reasonably likely to cause crashes. The Court held that even assuming the FAAAA's preemption provision in 49 U.S.C. section 14501(c)(1) would otherwise reach the negligent-hiring claim, the safety exception in section 14501(c)(2)(A) saves it because such a claim is one regulating safety 'with respect to motor vehicles.' Construing 'with respect to' to mean 'concerns' or 'regards,' the Court reasoned that requiring a broker to exercise ordinary care in selecting a carrier concerns the trucks that will transport the goods.
why: The decision resolves a circuit split and establishes that state-law negligent-hiring claims against freight brokers who select unsafe motor carriers are not preempted by the FAAAA, abrogating the contrary Eleventh Circuit rule that had governed in Georgia.
editor_note: The Supreme Court's resolution of the broker-preemption split, and the decision that abrogated the Eleventh Circuit's contrary rule in Aspen American v. Landstar Ranger. Assuming without deciding that the FAAAA's § 14501(c)(1) reaches a negligent-selection claim against a freight broker, the Court held the § 14501(c)(2)(A) safety exception saves it. The practical effect in Georgia federal court: the preemption defense that had foreclosed these claims against brokers is gone, and the Eleventh Circuit is already vacating judgments that relied on the old rule (the Hodge remand).

name: Docs of CT, LLC v. Biotek Services, LLC
synopsis: A party sought to vacate an arbitration award under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b), arguing that ex parte communications between the arbitrator and opposing counsel were per se prejudicial. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that to establish that its rights were prejudiced by one of the listed grounds for vacatur, the moving party must show that the challenged conduct affected or influenced the outcome of the arbitration, and that prejudice is not presumed outside rare contexts. Because the moving party offered no basis for concluding the ex parte communications affected the outcome, the Court affirmed.
why: This decision establishes that prejudice under OCGA section 9-9-13 (b) requires an outcome-focused showing of actual prejudice, so parties seeking to vacate arbitral awards must demonstrate how the challenged conduct affected the result rather than relying on per se or presumed prejudice.

name: Statham v. Quang
synopsis: After a patient was injured during a hysterectomy in which a medical student manipulated a sponge stick under the physicians' supervision, she sought to hold the supervising physicians vicariously liable for the student's negligence. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that OCGA section 51-1-38, which immunizes medical students from civil liability under certain circumstances, neither imposes vicarious liability on supervising physicians nor renders them immune from it, leaving their liability to be determined as otherwise provided by law. The Court further held that a physician may be vicariously liable under respondeat superior for a supervised medical student's negligence where the evidence shows the physician assumed actual control over the student's physical conduct, even absent a contractual right of control, and that the undisputed evidence here created a jury question on that issue.
why: The decision clarifies that a contract disclaiming an agency relationship is not dispositive of vicarious liability and that assumed control over an agent's physical conduct can independently establish a master-servant relationship for respondeat superior, an issue central to medical malpractice and agency law.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The Court held that the borrowed servant doctrine operates only as a defense to a respondeat superior claim, relieving a general master of liability when a special master had the right of control, and not as an independent basis for imposing vicarious liability on a defendant. A plaintiff seeking to hold a special master liable for a borrowed servant's conduct must establish the elements of respondeat superior rather than rely on the borrowed servant doctrine itself. The Court disapproved any reading of Hendley v. Evans to the contrary.
additional_holdings.why: This resolves how the borrowed servant doctrine functions, confining it to a defensive role and requiring plaintiffs to proceed under respondeat superior to impose vicarious liability.

name: Love v. McKnight
synopsis: Plaintiff sought expenses of litigation under OCGA section 13-6-11 based on bad faith after a rear-end collision in which defendant was cited and pleaded guilty to following too closely. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that bad faith under the statute requires conduct that is intentional, wanton, reckless, or at least indicative of conscious indifference to known harmful consequences, and that mere negligence does not suffice. The court held that the violation of a strict-liability traffic law, by itself, does not establish bad faith, and that evidence of distraction from cell phone use, raising at most an issue of negligence, was insufficient to submit the claim to the jury. The court reasoned that allowing litigation expenses in routine negligence cases would contradict the statute's prefatory language that expenses generally shall not be allowed.
why: This decision clarifies that bad faith under OCGA section 13-6-11 requires more than negligence or a traffic-law violation, setting the threshold for submitting litigation-expense claims to a jury in tort and auto cases.

name: Wasserman v. Franklin County
synopsis: Plaintiff sought to assert a third party's federal equal protection rights in Georgia courts under the federal doctrine of third-party standing. The Georgia Supreme Court held that the federal doctrine of third-party standing is not part of Georgia constitutional standing law, because the Judicial Power Paragraph of the Georgia Constitution requires a plaintiff, at a minimum, to assert a violation of her own legal rights to invoke a Georgia court's judicial power, and overruled Burgess and later decisions to the extent they adopted that doctrine. The Court also rejected the plaintiff's Supremacy Clause argument, holding that Georgia's constitutional standing requirement is a neutral jurisdictional rule that may be applied to bar a Section 1983 claim brought by someone asserting only a nonparty's rights. The Court vacated and remanded, leaving the plaintiff's separate assignment-of-claim theory for the courts below to address in the first instance.
why: It establishes that a Georgia plaintiff must assert a violation of her own legal rights to have standing and eliminates federal third-party standing as a basis for suing in Georgia courts, a threshold rule of broad importance to all civil litigators.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The plaintiff argued that applying Georgia's standing requirements to bar her federal Section 1983 claim would violate the Supremacy Clause. The Court held that Georgia's constitutional standing rule is a neutral jurisdictional rule that does not target or discriminate against federal causes of action, and so may be applied evenhandedly to bar a Section 1983 claim asserted by a plaintiff who alleges only a nonparty's rights.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that Georgia's constitutional standing requirement is a neutral jurisdictional rule enforceable against federal claims in state court without offending the Supremacy Clause.

name: Cook-Rose v. Waffle House, Inc.
synopsis: Plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed a premises liability suit, filed a renewal action under OCGA section 9-2-61(a), and then sought to appeal a post-dismissal attorneys' fees award entered in the dismissed case by filing a discretionary application. The Court of Appeals dismissed for failure to obtain a certificate of immediate review, reasoning that the pendency of the renewal action meant the case remained pending below. The Supreme Court held that a renewal action is a new case de novo, not a continuance of the dismissed action, so the pendency of the renewal did not keep the dismissed case pending. Because the fee order made the dismissed case no longer pending in the court below, it was a final judgment under OCGA section 5-6-34(a)(1) and no certificate of immediate review was required.
why: The decision clarifies that a post-dismissal attorneys' fees order in a case that has been voluntarily dismissed and renewed is a final judgment appealable by discretionary application without a certificate of immediate review, because the renewal action is a separate new case.

name: Whitaker Farms, LLC v. Fitzgerald Fruit Farms, LLC
synopsis: After a jury awarded punitive damages on a trespass claim, the defendant challenged the admission of statements its officer made during a settlement conference, which the Court of Appeals had upheld as admissible under OCGA section 24-4-408 (c) to show state of mind. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a request for punitive damages is a 'claim' within the meaning of Rule 408 (a), and that because a defendant's state of mind is an element of a punitive damages claim, evidence offered to prove that state of mind is offered to prove liability for the claim and is therefore inadmissible. The court did not decide whether Rule 408 (b) categorically excludes all statements made in compromise negotiations. The court vacated and remanded for the Court of Appeals to determine whether the erroneous admission was harmful.
why: The decision clarifies that settlement-conference statements cannot be admitted to prove a defendant's state of mind for purposes of establishing entitlement to punitive damages, because such evidence proves an element of, and thus liability for, the punitive damages claim under OCGA section 24-4-408 (a).

name: Titshaw v. Geer
synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a claim for breach of a contract for legal services may be governed by either the six-year statute of limitation in OCGA section 9-3-24 or the four-year statute in OCGA section 9-3-25, depending on whether the duty allegedly breached arose directly from a written contract, applying the framework set out in Newell Recycling. The Court clarified that the six-year period applies when the breach concerns a duty growing directly out of an enforceable written contract for legal services, including duties implied by law, while the four-year period applies when no written contract exists, the writing is unenforceable, or the breach relates only remotely to the written agreement. The Court disapproved broad readings of Armstrong v. Cuffie and Coe v. Proskauer Rose as suggesting that all breach-of-contract-for-legal-services claims are governed by the four-year period. The judgments were vacated and remanded.
why: The decision establishes that the Newell Recycling framework, not a single fixed limitation period, determines whether the six-year or four-year statute of limitation governs a breach-of-contract-for-legal-services claim.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The Court disapproved the Oehlerich/Smiley line of Court of Appeals cases holding that a claim is barred as duplicative of a legal-malpractice claim when it is based on the same conduct, the same damages, and duties from the same source. The Court held that plaintiffs may simultaneously pursue different causes of action with different elements arising from the same underlying conduct, and that a statute of limitation barring one cause of action does not necessarily bar other causes of action based on the same facts, because each claim must be analyzed separately to determine its applicable limitation period and accrual date.
additional_holdings.why: The decision confirms that a plaintiff may pursue alternative tort and contract theories arising from the same conduct, and that the timeliness of each claim must be assessed independently rather than treating one claim as duplicative of another.

name: Vest Monroe, LLC v. Doe
synopsis: A named plaintiff sought to certify a class of patients whose protected health information was disclosed by a former facility employee, and the trial court denied certification for lack of commonality and typicality. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in finding a lack of typicality under OCGA section 9-11-23 (a) (3), because the plaintiff's information consisted only of discharge summaries and census reports while other class members had clinical and diagnostic information disclosed, making the plaintiff's injury qualitatively different and subject to different theories of liability, proof, and defenses. The Court clarified that under the rigorous-analysis standard and abuse-of-discretion review, a factual variation defeats typicality when the representative's factual position markedly differs from that of other class members, even where all claims arise from the same general event. Because failure on typicality alone defeats certification, the Court did not reach commonality.
why: It clarifies that a class representative's claims can fail the typicality requirement when the representative's injury is qualitatively different from other class members' even though all arise from the same event, and reaffirms the deferential abuse-of-discretion scope of appellate review of class-certification rulings.

name: Golden v. Floyd Healthcare Management, Inc.
synopsis: Plaintiff filed a renewal medical malpractice action that defendant argued was barred by the five-year statute of repose in OCGA § 9-3-71 (b). The Supreme Court of Georgia held that OCGA § 38-3-62 (a) of the Judicial Emergency Act empowers an authorized judicial official to suspend, toll, extend, or otherwise grant relief from a statute of repose, because a repose period is a 'deadline' within the statute's non-exhaustive list. The Court further held that the March 14, 2020 COVID-19 emergency order and subsequent orders did toll OCGA § 9-3-71 (b), so plaintiff's claims were not time-barred. In reaching the first holding, the Court disapproved Simmons v. Sonyika and any other Georgia case to the extent they establish an absolute rule that a statute of repose can never be tolled under any circumstances.
why: This decision clarifies that Georgia statutes of repose are not categorically immune from tolling and that the Judicial Emergency Act's COVID-19 orders tolled the medical malpractice repose period, affecting the timeliness of claims filed during and after the pandemic.

additional_holdings.synopsis: Defendant argued that applying the tolling order to the repose statute would deprive it of vested due process rights that arose at the time of the allegedly negligent treatment in 2016. Applying Tampa Tank, the Court held that a defendant's vested right under a statute of repose arises only when the repose period would have expired and extinguished the plaintiff's claim, not when the negligent act occurred. Because the March 14 Order tolled the repose period before it would have expired in July 2021, the tolling did not deprive defendant of vested rights and was constitutional under the federal and Georgia Constitutions.
additional_holdings.why: The decision fixes the moment a defendant's repose-based due process rights vest at the expiration of the repose period rather than at the time of the alleged conduct, defining when legislative or emergency tolling may constitutionally reach a repose statute.

name: Waetzig v. Halliburton Energy Services, Inc.
synopsis: A plaintiff voluntarily dismissed his federal lawsuit without prejudice under Rule 41(a) and submitted his claims to arbitration, then sought to reopen the dismissed case under Rule 60(b) after losing at arbitration. The Supreme Court unanimously held that a Rule 41(a) voluntary dismissal without prejudice qualifies as a "final proceeding" under Rule 60(b), so a district court may use Rule 60(b) to reopen such a case. The Court rejected importing the appellate-jurisdiction concept of finality from 28 U.S.C. section 1291 into Rule 60(b), and read "judgment, order, or proceeding" as ascending in generality so that "proceeding" reaches all steps in an action. The Court expressly declined to decide whether the district court had jurisdiction over the motion to vacate the arbitration award, leaving that and the propriety of relief for remand.
why: It clarifies that a Rule 41(a) voluntary dismissal without prejudice is reachable under Rule 60(b), establishing the mechanism by which a litigant may ask a federal court to reopen a case that was voluntarily dismissed.

name: Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger
synopsis: Plaintiff sued in state court asserting both federal and state-law claims, and defendant removed based on the federal claim, with the state claims proceeding under supplemental jurisdiction. After removal, plaintiff amended the complaint to delete every federal-law claim and sought remand. A unanimous Court held that when a post-removal amendment excises the federal-law claims that enabled removal, leaving only state-law claims, the federal court loses supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1367 and must remand to state court, because section 1367 draws no distinction between original and removed cases and jurisdiction follows the amended, now operative, pleading. The Court treated the contrary statement in the Rockwell footnote as non-binding dictum that does not withstand analysis.
why: It establishes that a plaintiff who originally pleads federal claims alongside state-law claims can defeat federal jurisdiction after removal by amending to drop all federal claims, requiring remand to state court, which directly bears on removal and remand strategy whenever federal and state tort claims are pleaded together.

name: Merritt Island Woodwerx, LLC v. Space Coast Credit Union
synopsis: A credit union moved to compel arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act after the AAA declined to administer a consumer's demand because the credit union had not registered its arbitration clause or paid the required compliance fee. Applying Bedgood v. Wyndham, the Eleventh Circuit held that the credit union's failure to comply with its chosen arbitral forum's policies placed it in default under Section 3 and rendered relief under Sections 3 and 4 unavailable. The court further held that a co-plaintiff with an identical, already-rejected arbitration clause could rely on a futility showing and need not separately demand arbitration, and that the substitute-forum clause permitted resolution in court because a court is a forum.
why: It establishes that post-filing compliance with arbitral-forum registration requirements cannot cure a party's prior noncompliance that caused the forum to decline arbitration, so a party that delayed remedying a self-created barrier to arbitration cannot later compel it.

additional_holdings.synopsis: As to the co-plaintiff that never formally demanded arbitration, the court held that possessing an arbitration provision identical to one the AAA had already refused to administer supplied a sufficient evidentiary basis, in the form of the actual declination letter, to establish futility. That co-plaintiff was therefore not required to make its own arbitration demand before suing, and Section 3 relief was unavailable.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that a co-plaintiff holding the same already-rejected arbitration clause may rely on a futility showing supported by the prior declination letter rather than making a separate arbitration demand.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that under Section 4 of the FAA the credit union could not obtain an order directing arbitration. As to the plaintiff that had attempted to arbitrate, there was no failure, neglect, or refusal to arbitrate; as to the plaintiff that had not demanded arbitration, the credit union was aggrieved by its own noncompliance and the AAA's resulting declination, not by that plaintiff's conduct.
additional_holdings.why: It applies Section 4's causal requirement to deny an order compelling arbitration where the movant's own failure to comply with arbitral-forum policies, rather than the opposing party's conduct, caused the inability to arbitrate.

name: Prime Property and Casualty Insurance Company v. Kepali Group, Inc.
synopsis: Applying Florida law in a diversity action, the Eleventh Circuit held that a commercial automobile policy's after-acquired auto provision provided continuing coverage for a newly acquired vehicle once the insured gave the required notice within 30 days, because that provision listed only two conditions for coverage and did not make payment of an additional premium a condition precedent. The court rejected the insurer's argument that coverage expired at the end of the 30-day notice period for nonpayment, reasoning that nothing in the provision so stated and that the policy's integration clause barred reliance on extrinsic terms. The court further held that the policy's premium audit and cancellation provisions, not a common-law reasonable-time default, governed when any additional premium was due and how coverage could be terminated for nonpayment, and that the insurer's failure to perform a premium audit or follow the cancellation procedures left coverage in force. The court affirmed the district court's ruling that the insurer had a duty to defend.
why: It clarifies that under Florida law a commercial fleet policy's after-acquired auto provision triggers continuing coverage upon timely notice without requiring premium payment as a condition precedent, and that the policy's own premium audit and cancellation mechanisms control the timing and consequences of nonpayment.

name: Kinsale Insurance Company v. Pride of St. Lucie Lodge 1189, Inc.
synopsis: Applying Florida law in a diversity action, the Eleventh Circuit reversed summary judgment for the insurer on a common-law bad-faith claim premised on the insurer's failure to initiate settlement negotiations before suit was filed. The court held that, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmovants, a jury could reasonably find that liability was clear under the Powell rule on a negligent-security fact pattern where a bar's security simultaneously ejected two feuding groups into a dark, unmonitored parking lot and a fatal shooting followed within ten to fifteen minutes, with injuries far exceeding the policy sublimit. The court clarified that the Powell 'clear liability' standard is one part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis rather than a separate threshold to bad-faith liability, and that 'clear' liability means liability that is obvious or easily understood, not liability that is guaranteed.
why: It clarifies that the duty to initiate settlement negotiations where liability is clear is a component of the totality-of-the-circumstances bad-faith analysis rather than a separate threshold, and defines what 'clear' liability means, guidance relevant to practitioners handling insurer bad-faith and negligent-security matters under analogous frameworks.

name: Fu Wu v. Chun Liu
synopsis: A defendant removed a state-court action under 9 U.S.C. section 205 of the Federal Arbitration Act, invoking the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, and moved to compel arbitration. In a single order, the district court denied the motion to compel and remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding the defendant could not enforce the arbitration clause. The Eleventh Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. section 1447(d) bars appellate review of such an order because FAA section 16(a)(1)(C) contains no express statutory exception to the remand bar, and neither the matter-of-substantive-law exception nor the Waco exception applies when the arbitration ruling is intrinsic to the jurisdictional determination. The court reasoned that the denial of arbitration was a jurisdictional finding with no conclusive effect on the state action, leaving the state court free to revisit it.
why: The decision clarifies that a litigant cannot use the FAA's appeal-of-arbitration-denial provision to circumvent the section 1447(d) bar when the district court's arbitration ruling is bound up in a jurisdictional remand, defining the limits of appellate review of arbitration-based removal.

name: Various Insurers, Reinsurers and Retrocessionaires v. General Electric International, Inc.
synopsis: Insurers, suing as subrogees of a power plant owner after a turbine failure, resisted arbitration of claims against various General Electric entities under a services contract their subrogor never signed. Because the parties and the district court had litigated the question under federal common law, the Eleventh Circuit assumed without deciding that federal common law governs third-party-beneficiary status, and applying that test with reference to Section 302(1)(b) of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, held that the non-signatory plant owner was an intended third-party beneficiary of the services contract because the contract repeatedly named it as project owner and gave it explicit, unilateral rights, including the right to direct changes to the power train sets and to act in emergencies. As subrogees, the insurers stood in the owner's shoes and were therefore bound by the contract's arbitration clause.
why: The decision clarifies that under federal common law a non-signatory may be compelled to arbitrate as a third-party beneficiary when the contract names it and confers specific enforceable rights, and that a subrogee takes that obligation along with the subrogor's rights. The court expressly did not decide that federal common law supplies the rule, so the case is not authority on that choice-of-law question.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court separately addressed who decides arbitrability of the individual claims. It held that the services contract's incorporation of the International Chamber of Commerce Conciliation and Arbitration Rules, whose Article 6(4) empowers the arbitral body to decide whether arbitration shall proceed, clearly and unmistakably delegates questions of arbitrability to the arbitrator, extending the reasoning of Terminix from AAA rules to ICC rules.
additional_holdings.why: The holding establishes that incorporating ICC arbitration rules, like incorporating AAA rules, delegates the gateway question of arbitrability to the arbitrator rather than the court.

name: Liberty Surplus Insurance Corporation v. Kaufman Lynn Construction, Inc.
disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded
synopsis: Applying Florida law, the Eleventh Circuit construed a Course of Construction Exclusion in a commercial general liability policy, which barred coverage for property damage to any insured project during the course of construction until the project is completed. The court held that the undefined phrase until the project is completed unambiguously means the entire multi-phase project must be finished, not merely the portion that sustained damage, so water damage to completed buildings was excluded while other buildings remained under construction and old buildings remained to be demolished. The court declined to import the policy's products-completed operations hazard definition of completed work into the exclusion, reasoning that your work and project are not synonymous. The coverage ruling was affirmed.
why: It establishes how courts applying Florida law read a Course of Construction Exclusion in a CGL policy, holding that completion of the project means the entire project rather than the damaged component.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that an insured has Article III standing to pursue a reformation counterclaim based on mutual mistake even without a pending claim on the disputed portion of the policy. Assuming the reformation claim would succeed, the insured received a policy different from the one it bargained for and paid a premium not commensurate with the coverage provided, which is a concrete and particularized benefit-of-the-bargain economic injury, and the claim presents no ripeness problem because it rests on a past mutual mistake rather than contingent future events. The court reversed the dismissal of the reformation counterclaim and remanded.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that a reformation claim for an insurance policy may proceed in federal court before any claim is made on the disputed coverage, treating the discrepancy between the bargained-for and issued policy as a present injury.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that the insurer could not recover attorney's fees under Florida's offer-of-judgment statute, section 768.79, and Rule 1.442 because its settlement proposal failed to resolve all claims between the parties. By treating the insured's declaratory and breach-of-contract counterclaims as essentially monetary while omitting from the proposal its own mirror-image declaratory-judgment claim regarding coverage, the insurer failed to comply with the requirement that a proposal resolve all claims for monetary relief. The denial of fees was affirmed.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that under section 768.79 and Rule 1.442 a settlement proposal must resolve all claims between the parties, so a proponent that characterizes the opponent's declaratory claim as monetary cannot omit its own mirror-image declaratory claim from the proposal.

name: Wilson v. Hearos, LLC
synopsis: A plaintiff sued an earplug manufacturer in Georgia state court for product-related hearing loss, and a non-party parent company removed the case to federal court. The Eleventh Circuit held that removal by a non-party, which lacks statutory authority under 28 U.S.C. section 1441(a) to remove, is a waivable procedural defect under 28 U.S.C. section 1447(c) rather than a jurisdictional one, so long as the federal court would have had original subject matter jurisdiction had the case been filed there. Because complete diversity and the amount in controversy were satisfied and the plaintiff did not move to remand within 30 days, the objection was waived.
why: It establishes that a non-party's improper removal does not defeat subject matter jurisdiction and must be challenged within 28 U.S.C. section 1447(c)'s 30-day window or be waived, clarifying when a removal defect can be raised.

additional_holdings.synopsis: After removal, the plaintiff argued that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(m)'s 90-day service window displaced Georgia's service-and-diligence rule for statute-of-limitations purposes. The court held that Georgia's requirement, that service relate back to the filing date only if the plaintiff exercised diligence in perfecting service, is an integral part of the state statute of limitations and is therefore substantive law that continues to apply in federal court under Erie. Rule 4(m) sets only a procedural maximum time to serve and does not extend a state-defined limitations period, so the district court correctly applied Georgia's diligence standard to find the claims time barred.
additional_holdings.why: It confirms that Georgia's service-and-diligence tolling rule remains controlling after removal to federal court and is not displaced by Federal Rule 4(m), affecting how limitations defenses are litigated in diversity cases originating in Georgia.

name: Lubin v. Starbucks Corporation
synopsis: A former employee's spouse, who obtained health coverage as a dependent but never signed an arbitration agreement, brought a putative class action against the employer alleging deficient COBRA notices. The employer moved to compel arbitration under the wife's employment agreement. The Eleventh Circuit held that a non-signatory cannot be compelled to arbitrate under an agreement he did not sign, particularly where his claim arises from an independent federal statutory right rather than from the contract. The court also held that the agreement's delegation clause did not clearly and unmistakably commit arbitrability to the arbitrator because it conflicted with an exclusion clause carving out actions to compel arbitration, so the court, not the arbitrator, decided arbitrability.
why: It clarifies that an arbitration agreement's delegation clause does not provide the clear and unmistakable evidence needed to send arbitrability to the arbitrator when it conflicts with an exclusion clause for actions to compel arbitration, and that a non-signatory suing on an independent statutory right is not bound to arbitrate.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court applied Florida contract law to the employer's three theories for binding a non-signatory. It held that equitable estoppel did not apply because the non-signatory was not relying on or seeking the benefits of the wife's employment agreement, the third-party beneficiary doctrine did not apply because that doctrine binds a beneficiary only when he sues to enforce the contract, and the derivative-claim theory failed because the spouse's right to a COBRA notice under 29 U.S.C. section 1166(a)(4) is an independent statutory right rather than one derivative of the participant's right.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies the limits of the equitable estoppel, third-party beneficiary, and derivative-claim exceptions used to bind non-signatories to arbitration agreements under state contract law.

name: Schleider v. GVDB Operations, LLC
synopsis: Plaintiffs brought state-law survival and wrongful death claims under Florida's Assisted Living Facilities Act, alleging an assisted living facility failed to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Defendants removed under the federal officer removal statute and the PREP Act, and the district court remanded. The Eleventh Circuit held that defendants did not act under a federal officer for purposes of 28 U.S.C. section 1442(a)(1), because mere compliance with federal guidance and designation as critical infrastructure do not establish the required relationship of subjection, guidance, or control, nor assistance with a basic governmental task.
why: It clarifies that compliance with federal regulations and recommendations and a critical-infrastructure designation are insufficient to support federal officer removal, narrowing the availability of that removal route for private entities.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that the PREP Act does not completely preempt state-law negligence claims arising from a failure to implement COVID-19 countermeasures. Because the PREP Act's immunity requires a causal relationship to the administration or use of a covered countermeasure, omission-based claims alleging that no countermeasure was used lack the necessary nexus, and the Act's compensation fund does not create a general cause of action displacing all pandemic-related state claims.
additional_holdings.why: It establishes that complete preemption under the PREP Act does not reach state-law claims premised on the failure to administer or use a covered countermeasure, leaving such claims removable only on other grounds.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court held that the PREP Act's exclusive willful-misconduct cause of action does not completely preempt plaintiffs' state-law negligence claims under Florida Statute section 429.28. Because the willful-misconduct standard is more stringent than negligence and plaintiffs asserted a negligence theory resting on an independent legal duty, the claims were not purely creatures of the PREP Act and did not support removal. A dissent argued that the complaint's willful-misconduct allegations fell within the scope of the federal cause of action and supported jurisdiction over the entire suit.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that state-law negligence claims pleaded under an independent duty are not completely preempted by the PREP Act's willful-misconduct cause of action, even when the complaint also includes willful-misconduct allegations.

name: VFS Leasing Co. v. Markel Insurance Company
synopsis: An insurer issued five joint checks to a lessee insured and a lessor loss payee as nonalternative co-payees, but the drawee bank cashed them solely for the lessee without the loss payee's endorsement, and the loss payee sued the insurer for breach of contract.
