Applying the Griggs principle as explained in Coinbase, the court held that a timely notice of appeal from a remand order reviewable under 28 U.S.C. section 1447(d) automatically stays all district court proceedings, including the remand order itself, so that later state court proceedings are void for purposes of the appeal, and that the earlier mailing of the remand order to the state court does not defeat the stay because the district court retains jurisdiction to reconsider a reviewable remand order. The court denied the city's motion to dismiss and rejected the mootness argument based on the amended state court complaints.
why: It establishes in the Eleventh Circuit that an appeal from a remand order in a federal officer removal case operates as a self-executing stay of district court proceedings, so post-remand state court activity and amended pleadings do not affect appellate review, a position that diverges from the Ninth Circuit's discretionary-stay approach and aligns with the Fourth Circuit.

additional_holdings.synopsis: As an alternative ground for denying the motion to dismiss, the court held that the defendants did not waive their right to remove or to appeal the remand order by answering, moving to dismiss, and appearing at a hearing in state court after remand. Waiver principles reach substantial offensive or defensive action taken in state court before removal, and here the only conduct identified occurred after remand and after the plaintiff itself successfully asked the state court to lift its stay pending appeal. Under those circumstances the defendants had no practical choice but to participate.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that post-remand participation in state court litigation, particularly where the plaintiff obtained dissolution of a stay pending appeal, does not forfeit the right to appeal a remand order.

additional_holdings.synopsis: On the merits, the court held that removal under 28 U.S.C. section 1442(a)(1) was proper. The defendants were "acting under" the EPA because, unlike an ordinary regulated party merely complying with detailed regulation, they were carrying out remediation selected in an EPA Record of Decision and consent decree at a listed Superfund site, work the agency would otherwise have had to perform; the city's continuing nuisance and trespass claims premised on inadequate remediation were "for or relating to" those acts; and the defendants raised a colorable federal defense that CERCLA and the consent decree conflict-preempt the state tort remedies. The court also stated that, following the Supreme Court's Plaquemines Parish decision, the "causal connection" and "causal nexus" phrasing previously used for the second prong should be retired in favor of asking whether the challenged acts are closely connected to the performance of federal duties.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies when parties performing EPA-directed CERCLA cleanup may remove state tort suits to federal court and updates the Eleventh Circuit's articulation of the "for or relating to" prong of the federal officer removal test.

name: National Assisted Living Risk Retention Group v. Bishop
synopsis: An assisted living resident wandered from the facility in July 2012 and was killed crossing a highway. The facility manager telephoned the insurance agent to report the death and the ensuing state agency investigations, but no demand or suit was made until the estate filed a wrongful death action in 2014. After obtaining a $20 million judgment and an assignment of the insured's rights under the 2012 claims-made policy through proceedings supplementary, the estate sued the insurer for denying coverage and a defense. The First District held that the policy was unambiguously claims-made, that the manager's call was notice of an injury or occurrence rather than a claim as defined by the policy, and that regulatory agency inquiries about whether the facility carried statutorily required insurance were not claims or suits made on behalf of the injured person, so no claim was first made during the 2012 policy period; the final judgment for the estate was reversed.
why: The decision draws a clear line under a claims-made policy between reporting an occurrence that may later generate a claim and a claim actually being made, and holds that regulatory investigations and inquiries about proof of insurance do not constitute a claim on behalf of the injured person.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court separately held that the trial court's finding that the insurer failed to prove a valid retroactive cancellation for nonpayment did not resolve the coverage question. Even if the 2012 policy was never properly cancelled, it expired by its own terms in January 2013, so the claim first made in the 2014 wrongful death action fell outside the policy period and any extended discovery period, none of which the insured purchased despite notices offering it. The court declined to reach reformation or estoppel theories directed at the later policies because the estate had voluntarily dismissed those counts with prejudice and had never obtained an assignment of rights under them.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies that a defective cancellation does not extend a claims-made policy beyond its expiration date, and that the reporting window turns on the policy period plus any purchased extended discovery period.

name: RLI Insurance Company v. Lehman
disposition: vacated and remanded with instructions to enter summary judgment for the insurer
synopsis: An umbrella insurer sought a declaratory judgment that it owed no coverage for injuries an insured suffered in a car accident, relying on policy language conditioning coverage on the underlying insurance limits being "exhausted by payment of judgments or settlements." One underlying uninsured/underinsured motorist carrier paid its full $200,000 limit, while a second underlying carrier with a $500,000 UM limit initially denied the claim and later settled for $50,001. Applying Florida law and dictionary definitions of "exhaust," the Eleventh Circuit held that a settlement well below the underlying policy limits does not fully consume those limits and therefore does not satisfy the exhaustion clause. The court distinguished a Florida Third District Court of Appeal decision that had found exhaustion through a below-limits settlement, noting that the clause there referred to exhausting "all primary insurance" without reference to policy limits and that the decision did not analyze the plain meaning of "exhaust," and concluded there was persuasive indication the Florida Supreme Court would depart from it. The panel vacated the sua sponte summary judgment entered for the insureds and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for the insurer, without reaching whether the insureds maintained the required amount of underlying UM coverage.
why: The decision construes an umbrella policy exhaustion clause tied to "policy limits" as requiring full consumption of the underlying limits rather than any settlement of the underlying claim, and illustrates when a federal court sitting in diversity will decline to follow a state intermediate appellate decision on insurance interpretation.

name: Mt. Hawley Insurance Company v. H&M Builders, LLC
disposition: appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction
synopsis: An insurer sought a declaratory judgment that it owed no duty to defend or indemnify its insured in an underlying state-court wrongful death action, and the district court granted summary judgment to the insured on the duty to defend while reserving the indemnity question. While the insurer's interlocutory appeal was pending, the underlying state-court action settled and was dismissed. The Eleventh Circuit held the appeal no longer presented an actual controversy under the Declaratory Judgment Act and Article III, because a duty-to-defend dispute depends on an actual dispute over a present defense obligation, and it rejected the parties' arguments that potential recovery of defense costs on reversal or of attorney fees under Florida law on affirmance preserved a live dispute, noting also that parties cannot stipulate to federal jurisdiction.
why: It establishes that a duty-to-defend declaratory action becomes moot once the underlying action is settled and dismissed, and that the prospect of recouping defense costs or obtaining a fee award does not by itself supply a live controversy.

additional_holdings.synopsis: As an independent ground, the court held that a partial summary judgment order resolving a duty-to-defend claim is appealable under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(a)(1) only if the order has injunctive qualities, examined case by case from the order's language and the parties' claims and counterclaims. Examples include language mandating that the insurer provide a defense or pay defense costs, a ruling on an insurer's request for injunctive relief, or a ruling on an insured's counterclaim for declaratory or injunctive relief. Here the order contained no mandatory language directed at the insurer, the insurer sought no injunctive relief, and the insured filed no counterclaim, so there was no interlocutory jurisdiction. The court expressly declined to follow the unpublished Addison Insurance decision to the extent it could be read to treat any partial summary judgment order on the duty to defend as immediately appealable.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies when an interlocutory coverage ruling on the duty to defend may be appealed before final judgment, limiting section 1292(a)(1) appeals to orders with injunctive qualities.

additional_holdings.synopsis: As a third independent ground, the court noted that the district court had since dismissed the duty-to-indemnify claim as moot and entered final judgment, so any appeal was properly taken from that final judgment, into which prior non-final rulings merged. A concurring judge would have rested the dismissal solely on mootness and declined to join the alternative jurisdictional grounds.
additional_holdings.why: It confirms that entry of final judgment during a pending interlocutory appeal channels review to an appeal from the final judgment rather than the earlier non-final order.

name: Vainberg v. Florida Insurance Guaranty Association
synopsis: Insureds whose water-damage claim the insurer elected to repair sued for breach of the resulting Drew repair contract, and after the insurer's insolvency the Florida Insurance Guaranty Association was substituted as defendant and a consent judgment for policy limits was entered. The Fourth District held that a suit for breach of a Drew repair contract falls within the fee-shifting scope of section 627.428, Florida Statutes (2015), because such a contract exists solely by virtue of the insurer's exercise of a repair right granted by the policy and the dispute therefore arises under the policy. The court also relied on the statute's disjunctive reference to a 'policy or contract executed by the insurer,' reasoning that an election-to-repair letter is itself a contract executed by the insurer and that reading 'contract' as adding nothing would render it superfluous. The order denying fees was reversed and the case remanded to determine the amount.
why: The decision establishes that an insurer's election to repair does not remove a subsequent breach claim from the reach of section 627.428's one-way fee-shifting provision.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The court separately held that section 631.70, Florida Statutes (2022), did not bar fees because the guaranty association denied a portion of the claim 'by affirmative action, other than delay.' Distinguishing prior decisions in which the association was sued before it could investigate and was compelled to answer, the court noted that here the association was substituted into pending litigation, had the benefit of an automatic stay and two agreed extensions, and then voluntarily pleaded coverage-based affirmative defenses. The court identified a sustained course of conduct constituting affirmative denial: the pre-answer partial payment excluding ordinance-and-law line items, the coverage affirmative defenses, corporate-representative testimony that the claim was not covered, the pretrial stipulation, and a summary judgment motion asserting non-coverage. It also held that where the association is substituted mid-litigation, the relevant inquiry is whether it denied coverage by affirmative action at any point before retrial, not before suit was filed, and that post-answer litigation conduct may be considered.
additional_holdings.why: It clarifies how the 'denial by affirmative action' requirement applies when a guaranty association is substituted into pending litigation, including that post-answer litigation positions and partial claim payments can supply the affirmative denial.

name: Lineberger v. Newberry
synopsis: After prevailing in a quiet-title boundary dispute and having the judgment affirmed on appeal, the prevailing parties left a motion for attorney fees under OCGA section 9-15-14 pending for five years, taking no action until they filed a notice of hearing shortly before the five-year anniversary of the last written order. The trial court held the case stood automatically dismissed by operation of law under the five-year rule and that it therefore lacked jurisdiction over the fee motion. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that a pending OCGA section 9-15-14 motion is part of the original action rather than a separate case, so the case was not fully adjudicated and the exception excusing already-resolved cases from the five-year rule did not apply. Because no written order signed by the judge and filed with the clerk, including an order of continuance, was obtained within five years, the automatic dismissal took effect one day before the scheduled hearing.
why: The decision clarifies that an unresolved attorney fee motion keeps a case pending for purposes of the five-year automatic dismissal rule under OCGA section 9-11-41(e), so parties with fee motions outstanding after judgment must obtain a written order or continuance within five years or lose the trial court's jurisdiction to decide the motion.

name: Estancia US Limited Partnership v. Aji-Dawkins
synopsis: In a premises case arising from a fall when a PVC railing gave way at a hotel's second-story walkway, the trial court granted plaintiff leave to amend to add a punitive damages claim based on gross negligence. Applying the Florida Supreme Court's recent clarification of the section 768.72(1) evidentiary-sufficiency test, the Sixth DCA reviewed de novo, viewed the proffered record in the light most favorable to the claimant, and asked whether a reasonable person could conclude the defendant engaged in gross negligence as defined in section 768.72(2), together with the employer criteria of section 768.72(3). The court held the deposition testimony did not support the two pleaded bases, because the maintenance employee who described the railing as a breakaway product testified he did not tell the owner it was unsuitable until after the fall and never said he reported an earlier child-related railing failure to the owner, while the other employee testified no safety concerns were raised. The order permitting the amendment was reversed with instructions to vacate it, and the court separately directed that a copy of the opinion be sent to The Florida Bar based on trial counsel's misrepresentations of the deposition record at the hearing and in the proposed written order.
why: The decision applies the clarified section 768.72(1) standard for pleading punitive damages, confirming that the reviewing court does not weigh evidence but tests whether the proffered record itself, read favorably to the claimant, could support a finding of gross negligence under the statutory definitions and the employer-liability criteria.

name: Citizens Property Insurance Corporation v. Nekouee
synopsis: An insured demanded appraisal under his residential property policy, the appraisers agreed on the amount of loss, and the insured then refused to sign the insurer's appraisal award form and filed a declaratory judgment action seeking only a declaration about the form's enforceability and his rights under the policy, without seeking damages. The trial court denied the insurer's motion to dismiss for failure to give the presuit notice required by section 627.70152(3)(a), Florida Statutes. The Second District held that section 627.70152(1)'s application to "all suits arising under" a residential or commercial property insurance policy means all suits, including declaratory judgment actions that seek no monetary relief, and that the statutorily specified notice contents remain workable in that setting. The court found a departure from the essential requirements of law, granted certiorari, and quashed the order, noting that section 627.70152(5) directs dismissal without prejudice when the required notice was not given.
why: The decision establishes that Florida's presuit notice condition precedent for property insurance suits reaches declaratory judgment actions seeking no damages, so claimants must serve the statutory notice before filing any such action and courts must dismiss without prejudice when it is absent.

additional_holdings.synopsis: The insured separately argued that his suit did not "arise under" the policy within the meaning of section 627.70152(1), relying on arbitration cases that read "arising out of" or "arising under" narrowly to reach only disputes relating to interpretation and performance of the contract. The court concluded that even under that narrower construction the suit arises under the policy, because the insured alleged a bona fide controversy over policy terms and resolving whether the appraisal award form imposed extracontractual conditions requires interpreting the policy. The court also rejected reliance on personal injury protection precedent construing a differently worded notice statute limited to actions "for benefits."
additional_holdings.why: The holding clarifies that a dispute over the form or terms used to conclude an appraisal is a suit "arising under" the property policy for presuit notice purposes because its resolution turns on policy interpretation.
